'''Clark Landis''' (born 1956) is an American chemist, whose research focuses on organic and inorganic chemistry. He is currently a Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=landis {{!}} Department of Chemistry|url=https://www2.chem.wisc.edu/users/landis|access-date=2021-06-13|website=www2.chem.wisc.edu|language=en}}</ref> He was awarded the ACS [[List of American Chemical Society national awards|Award in Organometallic Chemistry]] in 2010,<ref name=":0" /> and is a fellow of the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name=":1" /> and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name=":2" />

== Education ==
In 1980, Landis received a Bachelor of Arts from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] (UIUC). At UIUC, he worked with Paul R. Robinson on ligand exchange reactions in molybdenum oxo complexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1979-01-01|title=Kinetics of the disproportionation of complexes of di-μ-oxo-bis[oxomolybdate(V)] in the presences of cyanide ion|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0020169300894554|journal=Inorganica Chimica Acta|language=en|volume=33|pages=63–67|doi=10.1016/S0020-1693(00)89455-4|issn=0020-1693|last1=Robinson|first1=Paul R.|last2=Landis|first2=Clark R.|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In 1983, he received his Ph.D. degree from the [[University of Chicago]]. At Chicago, Landis worked with Prof. [[Jack Halpern (chemist)|Jack Halpern]] on mechanistic studies of cationic rhodium catalysts that perform [[Hydrogenation|hydrogenation of alkenes]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Landis|first1=Clark R.|last2=Halpern|first2=Jack|date=1983|title=Homogeneous catalysis of arene hydrogenation by cationic rhodium arene journal|date=1983-07-05|title=Cationic rhodium hydrogenation catalysts containing chelating diphosphine ligands: effect of chelate ring size|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0022328X83850712|journal=Journal of Organometallic In 1986, Landis began his independent academic career at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]].<ref name=":3" /> He moved to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin-Madison]] in 1990 and has been a full Professor since 1997.<ref name=":3" />

==Research focuses==
Landis's research focuses on the asymmetric hydroformylation (AHF) of alkenes and alkynes through rhodium-based (Rh) catalysts with phosphine ligands. Rh catalysts with bisdiazaphospholane (BDP) ligands, shown in Figure 2, could convert substrates into highly enantio- and regio-specific [[aldehyde]] products. Landis and co-workers are also the inventors and patent holders of BDP and other diazaphosphacycle metal complexes.

===AHF===
[[Hydroformylation]] (AHF) converts alkenes to aldehydes. AHF has a wide range of industrial applications, including synthesizing linear aliphatic aldehydes. For example, making butanal from propene. Also, AHF is commercially used to synthesize aromatic aldehydes, including anti-inflammatory agents: ibuprofen and [[naproxen]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bourque|first1=S. Christine|last2=Maltais|first2=François|last3=Xiao|first3=Wen-Jing|last4=Tardif|first4=Olivier|last5=Alper|first5=Howard|last6=Arya|first6=Prabhat|last7=Manzer|first7=Leo E.|date=1999-04-01|title=Hydroformylation Reactions with Rhodium-Complexed Dendrimers on Silica|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=121|issue=13|pages=3035–3038|doi=10.1021/ja983764b|s2cid=94098155 |issn=0002-7863|url=https://nrc-publications.canada.ca/eng/view/accepted/?id=b8bd64ab-50a6-4265-b0ae-969332e9e3a7}}</ref>
[[File:General Asymmetric Hydroformylation Reaction.tif|center|thumb|378x378px|Figure 1: General Asymmetric Hydroformylation reaction of olefins to produce aldehydes.]]

===AHF is Stereospecific===
Wilkinson and Brown first discovered Rh-based catalysts in the 70s’. AHF of alkenes with Rh-based catalysts could yield high ratio of linear chain to branched chain aldehydes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brown|first1=C. K.|last2=Wilkinson|first2=G.|date=1970-01-01|title=Homogeneous hydroformylation of alkenes with hydridocarbonyltris-(triphenylphosphine)rhodium(I) as catalyst.|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society A: Inorganic, Physical, Theoretical|pages=2753–2764|language=en|doi=10.1039/J19700002753|issn=0022-4944}}</ref> Recent work from Landis group showed how AHF of non-linear compounds with Rh-based catalysts can produce stereospecific aldehydes.

=== Rh-BDP Catalysts and Alkenes ===
AHFs of alkenes, specifically enol esters and enamides, with Rh-BDP catalysts yield high concentration of stereo and regio-specific aldehydes. Adding extra functional groups to the alkenes does not interfere with specificity or degree of AHF.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Abrams|first1=M. Leigh|last2=Foarta|first2=Floriana|last3=Landis|first3=Clark R.|date=2014-10-15|title=Asymmetric Hydroformylation of Z-Enamides and Enol Esters with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=136|issue=41|pages=14583–14588|doi=10.1021/ja507701k|pmid=25241657|issn=0002-7863}}</ref>

===AHF is Affected by CO Concentration===
Complex alkenes with multiple branches and/or multiple chiral centers are more difficult to go through stereospecific AHF, compared to linear alkenes. NMR and IR spectroscopies indicate olefin substrates often rearrange their more substituted chains or carbonyl groups to increase the compounds' thermodynamic stability. CO concentration also affects the rate and probability of isomerization. CO concentration and the relatively complex reaction steps make assigning specific steps in metal-ligand catalyzed AHF as a rate or product determinant a more difficult task.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brezny|first1=Anna C.|last2=Landis|first2=Clark R.|date=2017-02-08|title=Unexpected CO Dependencies, Catalyst Speciation, and Single Turnover Hydrogenolysis Studies of Hydroformylation via High Pressure NMR Spectroscopy|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=EN|volume=139|issue=7|pages=2778–2785|doi=10.1021/jacs.6b12533|pmid=28125782}}</ref>

===AHF is Affected by Pressure===
Pressure also affects AHF of olefins by altering the kinetics in the reaction pathways. For example, [[styrene]] is converted to linear isomers under lower pressure but branched isomers under higher pressure.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tonks|first1=Ian A.|last2=Froese|first2=Robert D.|last3=Landis|first3=Clark R.|date=2013-12-06|title=Very Low Pressure Rh-Catalyzed Hydroformylation of Styrene with (S,S,S-Bisdiazaphos): Regioselectivity Inversion and Mechanistic Insights|journal=ACS Catalysis|volume=3|issue=12|pages=2905–2909|doi=10.1021/cs400943s}}</ref>

===Synthesis of BDP Ligand===
Bisdiazaphospholane (BDP) on Rh increases reactivity and enantioselectivity of olefin AHF. However, BDP is difficult to purify in its enantiopure form through common purification techniques, such as, [[column chromatography]]. Jones recently synthesized BDP, resulting in a scalable and commercial production. The processes include the synthesis of [[racemic mixture]] of tetracarboxylic acid, separation of an enantiomer by selective recrystallization of diastereomeric salts, amide bond formation, and crystallization of purified BDP. These processes produce high yield of pure BDP, so greater modification of Rh-BDP catalysts could enhance alkene AHF.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=Bradley R.|last2=Abrams|first2=M. Leigh|last3=Landis|first3=Clark R.|last4=May|first4=Scott A.|last5=Campbell|first5=Alison N.|last6=Martinelli|first6=Joseph R.|last7=Calvin|first7=Joel R.|date=2016-12-02|title=Scalable Synthesis of Enantiopure Bis-3,4-diazaphospholane Ligands for Asymmetric Catalysis|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=81|issue=23|pages=11965–11970|doi=10.1021/acs.joc.6b01915|pmid=27787982|issn=0022-3263}}</ref>

[[File:Bisdiazaphospholane (BDP).tif|thumb|Figure 2: Bisdiazaphospholane (BDP), the ligand for Rh-based catalyst.]]

===AHF Products Prediction===
A library of BDP derivatives with specific chiral center arrangement and substituents was made to study AHF on olefins. Structure of BDP affects the degree of enantio-, regio- selectivity, and branched:linear ratio of aldehyde products on a wide range of olefin reactants, including 2,3-dihydrofuran and styrene. The data collected helps with predicting the possible aldehyde products from olefin of interest.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Adint|first1=Tyler T.|last2=Wong|first2=Gene W.|last3=Landis|first3=Clark R.|date=2013-05-03|title=Libraries of Bisdiazaphospholanes and Optimization of Rhodium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Hydroformylation|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=78|issue=9|pages=4231–4238|doi=10.1021/jo400525w|pmid=23581247|issn=0022-3263}}</ref>

===Rh Catalyst can be Used to Synthesis Polyester===
Rh-based catalysts also polymerize carboxylic acids into oligo(2-hydroxyacid) s through hydroacyloxylation with alkynes. The oligomer is then modified to remove the alkenyl groups. AHF then converts the oligomer to aldehydes. This novel approach of polyester synthesis needs further adjustments to improve its efficiency so it may be industrially applicable.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Foarta|first1=Floriana|last2=Landis|first2=Clark R.|date=2016-11-18|title=Condensation Oligomers with Sequence Control but without Coupling Reagents and Protecting Groups via Asymmetric Hydroformylation and Hydroacyloxylation|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=81|issue=22|pages=11250–11255|doi=10.1021/acs.joc.6b02210|pmid=27766871|issn=0022-3263}}</ref>
